items.stem: State the principle of conservation of energy.
items.answer: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one store to another (total energy is constant).
items.markingKey: cannot be created or destroyed [1]; only transferred/total constant [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a bouncing ball rises to a lower height after each bounce, using the principle of conservation of energy.
items.answer: At each bounce some energy is transferred to the internal (thermal) store of the ball and floor and as sound, so less is left in the gravitational potential store at the top; the total energy is still conserved.
items.markingKey: energy dissipated as thermal/sound [1]; less GPE at top [1]; total conserved [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by saying that energy is "wasted" in an electric motor.
items.answer: Some of the input energy is transferred to stores that are not useful, such as the internal store of the motor and surroundings (by heating) and sound; it spreads out and cannot easily be used.
items.markingKey: transferred to non-useful stores [1]; dissipated to surroundings [1] [2]

items.stem: A hairdryer is supplied with 1200 J of energy and transfers 60 J usefully as thermal (of the air) and kinetic energy. Work out the energy wasted.
items.markingKey: wasted = 1200 − 60 = 1140 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A loudspeaker is supplied with 500 J. It transfers 25 J usefully and 380 J to the internal store of its surroundings by heating; the rest is transferred as sound. Calculate the energy transferred as sound and state the principle you used.
items.answer: 95 J; conservation of energy (total output = input).
items.markingKey: principle of conservation [1]; 500 − 25 − 380 [1] = 95 J [1] [3]

items.stem: Consider the moment when a stretched catapult fires a stone. (a) Describe how the energy is transferred. (b) Explain what happens to the wasted energy in the end.
items.answer: (a) Mechanically by the force of the elastic. (b) It is dissipated: spread out into the internal store of the surroundings, warming them slightly.
items.markingKey: (a) Mechanically by the force of the elastic (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) It is dissipated [1]; spread out into the internal store of the surroundings, warming them slightly [1] [2]

items.stem: In which store is energy held in a stretched spring?
items.answer: Elastic (strain)
items.markingKey: Deformed elastic objects store elastic (strain) energy.

items.stem: A student says "energy is used up when a torch battery goes flat". Explain why this is not correct.
items.answer: The energy is not destroyed; it has been transferred from the chemical store of the battery to the internal (thermal) store of the surroundings by light and heating.
items.markingKey: energy not destroyed [1]; transferred to surroundings [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the total energy of a system is the same before and after a transfer even when the transfer is inefficient.
items.answer: Energy is conserved: wasted energy goes into stores such as thermal energy of the surroundings; useful + wasted = total input.
items.markingKey: conservation [1]; useful + wasted = input [1] [2]

items.stem: An LED lamp is supplied with 2000 J of energy and transfers 1700 J usefully as light energy. Work out the energy wasted.
items.markingKey: wasted = 2000 − 1700 = 300 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A filament lamp is supplied with 2000 J. It transfers 100 J usefully and 1520 J to the internal store of its surroundings by heating; the rest is transferred as sound. Calculate the energy transferred as sound and state the principle you used.
items.answer: 380 J; conservation of energy (total output = input).
items.markingKey: principle of conservation [1]; 2000 − 100 − 1520 [1] = 380 J [1] [3]

items.stem: Consider the moment when a car brakes to a stop. (a) Describe how the energy is transferred. (b) Explain what happens to the wasted energy in the end.
items.answer: (a) Mechanically by friction, then by heating. (b) It is dissipated: spread out into the internal store of the surroundings, warming them slightly.
items.markingKey: (a) Mechanically by friction [1]; then by heating [1] [2] (b) It is dissipated [1]; spread out into the internal store of the surroundings, warming them slightly [1] [2]

items.stem: Consider the moment when a bow is used to shoot an arrow upwards. (a) Name the store that energy is transferred from. (b) 500 J leaves the first store and 200 J is wasted. Calculate the useful energy transferred. (c) Explain what happens to the wasted energy in the end.
items.answer: (a) Elastic (strain). (b) 300 J (c) It is dissipated: spread out into the internal store of the surroundings, warming them slightly.
items.markingKey: (a) Elastic (strain) [1] (b) conservation of energy (method/substitution) [1]; answer 300 J with unit [1] [2] (c) It is dissipated [1]; spread out into the internal store of the surroundings, warming them slightly [1] [2]

items.stem: Which equation gives kinetic energy?
items.answer: Eₖ = ½mv²
items.markingKey: Kinetic energy = ½ × mass × speed².

items.stem: Explain why a car travelling at 60 km/h needs much more than twice the braking distance of one at 30 km/h.
items.answer: Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, so at double the speed it has four times the kinetic energy; with the same braking force, about four times the distance is needed.
items.markingKey: KE ∝ v² [1]; four times energy, distance ∝ energy [1] [2]

items.stem: A ball is thrown upwards. Describe the energy changes as it rises and falls, ignoring air resistance.
items.answer: Rising: kinetic store decreases and gravitational potential store increases; at the top KE is minimum; falling: GPE transferred back to KE; total constant.
items.markingKey: rising KE → GPE [1]; falling GPE → KE [1]; total constant [1] [3]

items.stem: A dog of mass 13 kg moves at 7.5 m/s. Work out the kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: Eₖ = ½mv² = ½ × 13 × 7.5² = 366 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A cyclist with bicycle of mass 79 kg has 2530 J of kinetic energy. Calculate its speed.
items.answer: 8 m/s

items.stem: A train carriage of mass 25 800 kg changes speed from 13 m/s to 26 m/s. (a) Calculate the kinetic energy at each speed. (b) Calculate the change in kinetic energy. (c) State how many times larger or smaller the kinetic energy has become and explain why this is not the same as the speed ratio.
items.answer: (a) 2 180 000 J and 8 710 000 J (b) 6 530 000 J gained (c) × 4: KE ∝ v², so the ratio is the square of the speed ratio (2).
items.markingKey: (a) both KEs [2] (b) difference [1] (c) ratio with v² reasoning [1] [4]

items.stem: A roller-coaster car of mass 400 kg starts from rest at the top of a track 5 m high (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the GPE lost in reaching the bottom. (b) Explain why the actual speed does not depend on the mass if the same percentage is wasted.
items.answer: (a) 19 600 J (b) Both GPE and KE are proportional to m, so m cancels.
items.markingKey: (a) mgΔh (method/substitution) [1]; answer 19 600 J with unit [1] [2] (b) Both GPE and KE are proportional to m [1]; so m cancels [1] [2]

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.5 kg starts from rest at the top of a long slope 20 m high (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) In fact 10% of the energy is transferred to thermal stores. Calculate the actual speed at the bottom. (b) Explain why the actual speed does not depend on the mass if the same percentage is wasted.
items.answer: (a) 18.8 m/s (b) Both GPE and KE are proportional to m, so m cancels.
items.markingKey: (a) KE = 88.2 J [1]; v [2] [3] (b) Both GPE and KE are proportional to m [1]; so m cancels [1] [2]

items.stem: Which equation gives the change in gravitational potential energy?
items.answer: ΔEₚ = mgΔh
items.markingKey: ΔGPE = mass × g × change in height.

items.stem: If the speed of a car doubles, its kinetic energy …
items.answer: becomes four times larger
items.markingKey: Eₖ ∝ v², so 2² = 4.

items.stem: Explain why the speed of an object falling from a height h (without air resistance) does not depend on its mass.
items.answer: mgh = ½mv², so m cancels and v = √(2gh).
items.markingKey: equates GPE and KE [1]; mass cancels [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the actual speed of a falling object is less than that calculated from mgh = ½mv².
items.answer: Air resistance does work on the object, transferring some energy to the internal store of the air and object, so less is transferred to kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: air resistance [1]; energy dissipated not to KE [1] [2]

items.stem: Consider a skier on a chairlift: mass 87 kg, raised through 169 m (g = 9.8 N/kg). Work out the gain in gravitational potential energy.
items.markingKey: ΔEₚ = mgΔh = 87 × 9.8 × 169 = 144 000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A lorry of mass 9620 kg moves at 17 m/s. Work out the kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: Eₖ = ½mv² = ½ × 9620 × 17² = 1 390 000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A car of mass 1000 kg changes speed from 18 m/s to 27 m/s. (a) Calculate the kinetic energy at each speed. (b) Calculate the change in kinetic energy. (c) State how many times larger or smaller the kinetic energy has become and explain why this is not the same as the speed ratio.
items.answer: (a) 162 000 J and 365 000 J (b) 203 000 J gained (c) × 2.25: KE ∝ v², so the ratio is the square of the speed ratio (1.5).
items.markingKey: (a) both KEs [2] (b) difference [1] (c) ratio with v² reasoning [1]; correct ratio value [1] [5]

items.stem: A skateboarder of mass 55 kg starts from rest at the top of a ramp 5 m high (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the GPE lost in reaching the bottom. (b) Calculate the speed at the bottom if no energy is wasted.
items.markingKey: (a) mgΔh (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2700 J with unit [1] [2] (b) mgh = ½mv² [1]; v = √(2gh) [1] [2]

items.stem: A roller-coaster car of mass 400 kg starts from rest at the top of a track 5 m high (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the speed at the bottom if no energy is wasted. (b) In fact 30% of the energy is transferred to thermal stores. Calculate the actual speed at the bottom.
In a Sankey diagram, what does the width of each arrow represent?
options: The speed of the energy transfer
items.answer: The amount of energy transferred
items.markingKey: Widths are drawn to scale with energy.

items.stem: Explain why the Sankey diagram for an LED lamp would look different from that for a filament lamp of the same light output.
items.answer: The LED wastes much less energy as heat, so its wasted arrow would be much narrower and the input arrow narrower for the same useful light.
items.markingKey: LED wastes less [1]; narrower wasted arrow / input [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how to draw a Sankey diagram to scale for a device.
items.answer: Choose a scale (e.g. 1 mm = 10 J); draw the input arrow with width for the total input; split into the useful arrow straight on and wasted arrows bending away, each with width proportional to its energy, so the widths add to the input.
items.markingKey: scale [1]; useful straight, wasted bent [1]; widths add to input [1] [3]

items.stem: A Sankey diagram for a kettle shows an input of 1000 J of electrical energy, 100 J wasted as thermal (of the kettle and air), 20 J wasted as sound and a useful output as thermal (of the water). Calculate the useful energy output.
items.markingKey: useful = 1000 − 100 − 20 = 880 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A Sankey diagram for a electric motor shows an input of 1000 J of electrical energy, 250 J wasted as thermal, 50 J wasted as sound and a useful kinetic output. The diagram is drawn with 1 mm representing 50 J. Calculate the useful output and the width of its arrow.

A television is supplied with 2000 J. It wastes 1200 J as thermal. (a) Calculate the useful light and sound output. (b) Explain what eventually happens to all of the energy output. (c) Suggest how the device could be made more efficient.
items.answer: (a) 800 J (b) It is dissipated to the internal store of the surroundings. (c) Reduce the wasted transfers, e.g. lubricate/insulate/use a more efficient technology.
items.markingKey: (a) 800 J [1] (b) It is dissipated to the internal store of the surroundings [1] (c) Reduce the wasted transfers [1]; e.g. lubricate/insulate/use a more efficient technology [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a Sankey diagram shows the efficiency of a device.
items.answer: Efficiency = width of useful output arrow ÷ width of input arrow; the wider the useful arrow relative to the input, the more efficient.
items.markingKey: ratio useful/input widths [1]; wider useful = more efficient [1] [2]

items.stem: Draw (describe) an energy transfer diagram for the following: a car brakes to a stop. Label the stores and the transfer pathway.
items.answer: Kinetic store → (mechanically by friction, then by heating) → internal (thermal) of the brakes and surroundings store, with a branch to the thermal store of the surroundings (wasted).
items.markingKey: starting store [1]; final store [1] [2]

items.stem: Draw (describe) an energy transfer diagram for the following: a ball is dropped and falls towards the ground. Label the stores and the transfer pathway.
items.answer: Gravitational potential store → (mechanically by the force of gravity) → kinetic store, with a branch to the thermal store of the surroundings (wasted).
items.markingKey: correct starting store [1]; correct useful final store [1]; pathway/wasted branch [1] [3]

items.stem: A Sankey diagram for a loudspeaker shows an input of 500 J of electrical energy, 450 J wasted as thermal and a useful output as sound. Determine the useful energy output.
items.markingKey: useful = 500 − 450 = 50 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A Sankey diagram for a solar panel shows an input of 1000 J of electrical energy, 800 J wasted as thermal and reflected light and a useful electrical output. The diagram is drawn with 1 mm representing 100 J. Calculate the useful output and the width of its arrow.

A kettle is supplied with 2000 J. It wastes 200 J as thermal (of the kettle and air) and 40 J as sound. (a) Calculate the useful thermal (of the water) output. (b) Explain what eventually happens to all of the energy output. (c) Suggest how the device could be made more efficient.
items.answer: (a) 1760 J (b) It is dissipated to the internal store of the surroundings. (c) Reduce the wasted transfers, e.g. lubricate/insulate/use a more efficient technology.
items.markingKey: (a) 1760 J [1] (b) It is dissipated to the internal store of the surroundings [1] (c) Reduce the wasted transfers [1]; e.g. lubricate/insulate/use a more efficient technology [1] [2]

items.stem: A coal-fired power station is supplied with 2000 J. It wastes 1240 J as thermal (cooling towers and flue gases). (a) Calculate the efficiency. (b) Describe the Sankey diagram for this device, using a scale of 1 mm to 20 J. (c) Explain what eventually happens to all of the energy output.
items.answer: (a) 38% (b) Input 100 mm wide; useful 38 mm straight on; wasted arrows 62 mm bending away. (c) It is dissipated to the internal store of the surroundings.
items.markingKey: (a) correct method/substitution [1]; answer 38% with unit [1] [2] (b) widths correct [2]; layout [1] [3] (c) It is dissipated to the internal store of the surroundings [1]

items.stem: Which equation gives efficiency?
options: efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input (× 100%)
items.answer: efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input (× 100%)
items.markingKey: Efficiency compares useful output with total input.

items.stem: Explain why LED lamps are replacing filament lamps.
items.answer: LEDs transfer a much higher proportion of electrical energy to light and less to thermal energy, so they are more efficient, cheaper to run and last longer.
items.markingKey: higher efficiency/less heating [1]; cheaper to run [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why efficiency has no unit.
items.answer: It is a ratio of two energies (J/J), so the units cancel.
items.markingKey: ratio of same quantity [1]

items.stem: A LED lamp is supplied with 1000 J and transfers 800 J usefully as light. Calculate the efficiency.
items.markingKey: efficiency = 800/1000 × 100 = 80%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A petrol car engine has an efficiency of 25%. Calculate the energy input needed for a useful kinetic output of 600 J, and the energy wasted.
items.answer: 2400 J; 1800 J wasted
items.markingKey: input = useful/efficiency [1] = 600/0.25 = 2400 J [1]; wasted = 1800 J [1] [3]

items.stem: A LED lamp is supplied with 2000 J. It wastes 400 J as thermal (heating surroundings). (a) Calculate the efficiency. (b) Suggest how the device could be made more efficient.
items.answer: (a) 80% (b) Reduce the wasted transfers, e.g. lubricate/insulate/use a more efficient technology.
items.markingKey: (a) correct method/substitution [1]; answer 80% with unit [1] [2] (b) Reduce the wasted transfers [1]; e.g. lubricate/insulate/use a more efficient technology [1] [2]

items.stem: A device has an efficiency of 0.25. What does this mean?
options: 25% of the input energy is transferred usefully
The device wastes 25% of the input
items.answer: 25% of the input energy is transferred usefully
items.markingKey: 0.25 = 25% useful; 75% wasted.

items.stem: A student says a 95% efficient heater is better than a 30% efficient lamp. Explain why comparing these efficiencies is not useful.
items.answer: They have different useful outputs (thermal vs light); for a heater nearly all energy becomes thermal energy, which is its useful output, so efficiency only compares devices with the same purpose.
items.markingKey: different useful outputs [1]; compare like with like [1] [2]

items.stem: Lina says a machine that takes in 1000 J and gives out 350 J of useful energy has an efficiency of 286%. Identify the error and give the correct value.
items.answer: Lina divided input by output; efficiency = 350/1000 × 100 = 35%. A value over 100% is impossible.
items.markingKey: inverted ratio [1]; 35% [1]; >100% impossible [1] [3]

items.stem: A filament lamp is supplied with 400 J and transfers 40 J usefully as light. What is the efficiency?
A solar panel is supplied with 1000 J and transfers 200 J usefully as electrical. Work out the efficiency.
items.markingKey: efficiency = 200/1000 × 100 = 20%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A coal-fired power station has an efficiency of 38%. Calculate the energy input needed for a useful electrical output of 60 MJ, and the energy wasted.
items.answer: 158 MJ; 97.9 MJ wasted
items.markingKey: input = useful/efficiency [1] = 60/0.38 = 158 MJ [1]; wasted = 97.9 MJ [1] [3]

items.stem: In which store is energy held in food and fuels?
items.answer: Chemical
items.markingKey: Chemical energy is released in reactions such as burning or respiration.

items.stem: Describe the energy transfers that take place when a solar-powered calculator works. Name the stores involved and how the energy is transferred.
items.answer: Energy is transferred from the nuclear (in the Sun) store to the internal (thermal) of the surroundings store, by radiation (light) and electrically. Some energy is dissipated to the surroundings.
items.markingKey: initial store [1]; final store [1] [2]

items.stem: A filament lamp is supplied with 1000 J of energy and transfers 750 J usefully as light energy. Calculate the energy wasted.
items.markingKey: wasted = 1000 − 750 = 250 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A loudspeaker is supplied with 800 J. It transfers 680 J usefully and 96 J to the internal store of its surroundings by heating; the rest is transferred as sound. Calculate the energy transferred as sound and state the principle you used.
items.answer: 24 J; conservation of energy (total output = input).
items.markingKey: principle of conservation [1]; 800 − 680 − 96 [1] = 24 J [1] [3]

items.stem: Consider the moment when a solar-powered calculator works. (a) Name the useful store that energy is transferred to. (b) Describe how the energy is transferred. (c) 400 J leaves the first store and 120 J is wasted. Calculate the useful energy transferred.

items.stem: Which is NOT a way of transferring energy between stores?
options: By changing the mass of an object without any force
By a force moving an object (mechanical work)
items.answer: By changing the mass of an object without any force
items.markingKey: Transfers are by forces (mechanical work), electrical currents, heating, and waves (light, sound).

items.stem: Describe the energy transfers that take place when a person climbs a flight of stairs. Name the stores involved and how the energy is transferred.
items.answer: Energy is transferred from the chemical (in the muscles) store to the gravitational potential store, mechanically by forces from the muscles. Some energy is dissipated to the surroundings.
items.markingKey: initial store [1]; final store [1] [2]

items.stem: An LED lamp is supplied with 200 J of energy and transfers 60 J usefully as light energy. Calculate the energy wasted.

items.stem: An LED lamp is supplied with 500 J. It transfers 375 J usefully and 88 J to the internal store of its surroundings by heating; the rest is transferred as sound. Calculate the energy transferred as sound and state the principle you used.

items.stem: Consider the moment when a rocket launches. (a) Name the store that energy is transferred from. (b) Name the useful store that energy is transferred to. (c) Describe how the energy is transferred. (d) Explain why the wasted energy is hard to use again.
items.answer: (a) Chemical. (b) Kinetic and gravitational potential. (c) Mechanically by thrust, and by heating. (d) It is spread thinly over a large amount of matter at low temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) Chemical [1] (b) Kinetic and gravitational potential [1] (c) Mechanically by thrust [1]; and by heating [1] [2] (d) It is spread thinly over a large amount of matter at low temperature [1]

items.stem: A 4 kg object moves at 3 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a car travelling at 60 km/h needs much more than twice the braking distance of one at 30 km/h. (b) Explain why the speed of an object falling from a height h (without air resistance) does not depend on its mass.
items.answer: (a) Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, so at double the speed it has four times the kinetic energy; with the same braking force, about four times the distance is needed. (b) mgh = ½mv², so m cancels and v = √(2gh).
items.markingKey: (a) KE ∝ v² [1]; four times energy, distance ∝ energy [1] [2] (b) equates GPE and KE [1]; mass cancels [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a car travelling at 60 km/h needs much more than twice the braking distance of one at 30 km/h. (b) Explain why the actual speed of a falling object is less than that calculated from mgh = ½mv².
items.answer: (a) Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, so at double the speed it has four times the kinetic energy; with the same braking force, about four times the distance is needed. (b) Air resistance does work on the object, transferring some energy to the internal store of the air and object, so less is transferred to kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: (a) KE ∝ v² [1]; four times energy, distance ∝ energy [1] [2] (b) air resistance [1]; energy dissipated not to KE [1] [2]

items.stem: Consider a skier on a chairlift: mass 89 kg, raised through 240 m (g = 9.8 N/kg). Determine the gain in gravitational potential energy.
items.markingKey: ΔEₚ = mgΔh = 89 × 9.8 × 240 = 209 000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A football of mass 0.43 kg moves at 17 m/s. Determine the kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: Eₖ = ½mv² = ½ × 0.43 × 17² = 62.1 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A skateboarder of mass 55 kg starts from rest at the top of a ramp 5 m high (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the speed at the bottom if no energy is wasted. (b) Explain why the actual speed does not depend on the mass if the same percentage is wasted.
items.answer: (a) 9.9 m/s (b) Both GPE and KE are proportional to m, so m cancels.
items.markingKey: (a) mgh = ½mv² [1]; v = √(2gh) [1] [2] (b) Both GPE and KE are proportional to m [1]; so m cancels [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a Sankey diagram, wasted energy is usually shown … (b) Why must the total width of the output arrows equal the width of the input arrow?
items.answer: (a) by arrows bending downwards (or away) from the main arrow (b) Energy is conserved
items.markingKey: (a) Useful output continues straight on; wasted outputs bend away. (b) Input = useful + wasted.

items.stem: Draw (describe) an energy transfer diagram for the following: a wind-up toy car runs across the floor. Label the stores and the transfer pathway.
items.answer: Elastic (strain) store → (mechanically) → kinetic, then internal (thermal) store, with a branch to the thermal store of the surroundings (wasted).
items.markingKey: correct starting store [1]; correct useful final store [1]; pathway/wasted branch [1] [3]

items.stem: A Sankey diagram for a electric motor shows an input of 1200 J of electrical energy, 300 J wasted as thermal, 60 J wasted as sound and a useful output as kinetic. Calculate the useful energy output.
items.markingKey: useful = 1200 − 300 − 60 = 840 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A Sankey diagram for a solar panel shows an input of 200 J of electrical energy, 160 J wasted as thermal and reflected light and a useful electrical output. The diagram is drawn with 1 mm representing 10 J. Calculate the useful output and the width of its arrow.
items.answer: 40 J; 4 mm

items.stem: A television is supplied with 1000 J. It wastes 600 J as thermal. (a) Describe the Sankey diagram for this device, using a scale of 1 mm to 20 J. (b) Explain what eventually happens to all of the energy output. (c) Suggest how the device could be made more efficient.
items.answer: (a) Input 50 mm wide; useful 20 mm straight on; wasted arrows 30 mm bending away. (b) It is dissipated to the internal store of the surroundings. (c) Reduce the wasted transfers, e.g. lubricate/insulate/use a more efficient technology.
items.markingKey: (a) widths correct [2]; layout [1] [3] (b) It is dissipated to the internal store of the surroundings [1] (c) Reduce the wasted transfers [1]; e.g. lubricate/insulate/use a more efficient technology [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why LED lamps are replacing filament lamps. (b) A student says a 95% efficient heater is better than a 30% efficient lamp. Explain why comparing these efficiencies is not useful.
items.answer: (a) LEDs transfer a much higher proportion of electrical energy to light and less to thermal energy, so they are more efficient, cheaper to run and last longer. (b) They have different useful outputs (thermal vs light); for a heater nearly all energy becomes thermal energy, which is its useful output, so efficiency only compares devices with the same purpose.
items.markingKey: (a) higher efficiency/less heating [1]; cheaper to run [1] [2] (b) different useful outputs [1]; compare like with like [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun says a machine that takes in 200 J and gives out 50 J of useful energy has an efficiency of 400%. Identify the error and give the correct value.
items.answer: Arjun divided input by output; efficiency = 50/200 × 100 = 25%. A value over 100% is impossible.
items.markingKey: inverted ratio [1]; 25% [1]; >100% impossible [1] [3]

items.stem: A kettle is supplied with 500 J and transfers 440 J usefully as thermal (of the water). Calculate the efficiency.
items.markingKey: efficiency = 440/500 × 100 = 88%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A LED lamp is supplied with 500 J. It wastes 100 J as thermal (heating surroundings). (a) Calculate the efficiency. (b) Suggest how the device could be made more efficient.
items.answer: (a) 80% (b) Reduce the wasted transfers, e.g. lubricate/insulate/use a more efficient technology.
items.markingKey: (a) correct method/substitution [1]; answer 80% with unit [1] [2] (b) Reduce the wasted transfers [1]; e.g. lubricate/insulate/use a more efficient technology [1] [2]
